question: How should Muslims fast in lands near the poles where the days are extremely long or the sun never sets?
asked: Brother Ghulam from Norway says the days there get exceedingly long, and in some parts of Norway the sun does not even set. How should fasting be done in lands that have no sunrise or sunset and are extremely close to the North or South Pole?
answer:
So this question comes to us from the other side of the world, from a land far, far away. And on a personal anecdote, I actually visited Norway. When I went to Norway, I intentionally took a trip to the northernmost city that had a masjid at the time (and I heard that after that time there's a masjid that is even more north than that). And I visited, this is 2014 (I believe there's a YouTube video; just Google my name and Norway), and the city is called Tromso, T-R-O-M-S-O. So I wanted to visit the masjid that is the closest to the North Pole; I took a trip specifically to go visit that masjid. There's a small musalla. I gave the khutbah there and interacted with... there were at least 150 people in the masjid over there. So I visited this land and the northernmost masjid in the world. Then I found out that a few years ago, a community in a city or village above them also built a masjid, mashallah, tabarakallah. Look where Islam has spread around the globe.

And when I visited Tromso, it was interesting to see that all of the houses, their windows (and I lived in one of the brothers' houses over there, I spent the night over there), their windows have special shutters that, when you press the button, it becomes 100% dark. And I said, what is the need for this? And he said that for most of the year, either there is perpetual sunlight or there is no sunlight whatsoever. For four to five months of the year, the sun is up. Then there's a month or two in which there's a little bit of day and night, and then the next four or five months there is no sun whatsoever. So if you wake up at 2 a.m., the sun will be above you.

And in that time frame... I went in the winter months, so it was a little bit of night and then most of it was dark. But if you go in the middle of the summer or in the middle of the winter, it will be full sunlight or full darkness. And if you look at the sun in the summertime, it won't go up and down. It's amazing: the sun will go round above you. If you look up at one time, it's going to be there, and then there, there, there; it's just going to go round in a circle. That's how the sun rises and sets, right? This is in the northernmost; this is not in the capital, Oslo, but up north in Tromso and other places close to the North Pole.

Now, our brother is asking what is to be done in those lands where the days of the fast are extremely long, or maybe there is even no sunrise and sunset. And the response to this: this is a very, very convoluted topic, and there are over 10 opinions on this issue, no exaggeration. And once again, like I explained in my last Q&A (for those of you watching this as a separate clip, the previous Q&A was about the degrees of Fajr), the same thing I said there I will say here, which is that all of this Q&A for today is for information purposes only, just for you to know. At the end of the day, you will follow your local shaykh, you will follow your local masjid and community, you will follow what your people are doing.

This is just for information purposes, for those that are living far away, or if a community or a board member is in charge and they don't know any better. They can listen to some advice from many people; this is one of the advices they will listen to, and then they can make an informed decision if they are the ones in charge. Otherwise, the average Muslim simply follows their local authorities, especially when it comes to these types of culture-sensitive issues. I have always said that: stick with your local ulama for the specifics. I can speak generics, and I will speak generics, and I'll give you a number of opinions that are well known in the global community. But at the end of the day, my own personal opinion is that you should not listen to my opinion. You should listen to the opinion of ulama who live amongst you and who understand the dynamics and the pros and cons in a better manner.

I don't live amongst you. And therefore, I might have, and I do have, my own hypothetical, what I consider to be the strongest position, but I hesitate to tell you to do it, because I don't live in your lands, and I want you to follow trained ulama, reputable ulama who live in your lands. If you have an 'alim in your town or village up north in Norway, follow them. If not, the local communities closest to you, or in Oslo or other places; there are plenty of scholars in Oslo, I've met a number of them. So you should go to those ulama and find out from them, because they understand the situation far better than I do, because they live amongst you.

So again, the answer today is for educational purposes, for information purposes. I'm not telling you specifically which one you should follow. That is something that is culturally sensitive, and there are perhaps dynamics I'm not fully aware of, and there are perhaps issues that I'm not cognizant of, because I'm speaking to you from another land.

Nonetheless, for information purposes, it's interesting for the rest of us to know. This is not a new issue. In fact, even in the Ottoman times there was a lot of back and forth, because the Ottomans conquered what they called the Balkan lands, and they knew of these lands where the sun did not rise or did not set. And so Ottoman muftis in the Hanafi madhhab gave some fatwas here and there, and it trickled down to the other madhhabs as well. So you do find a little bit of discussion. However, in modern times, obviously, this issue has been discussed a lot more, and many fatwa councils and many ulama around the globe have opined on this issue, and so there are a number of opinions on this issue.

And of course, before we begin, realize that we're actually talking about multiple scenarios all at once. The first scenario is that there is a sunrise and sunset, but it's very long. So maybe the fast is 19 hours, 20 hours. Maybe there's a place, I believe in Finland, where the sun does rise and set, but the day is 22 hours long. So that's a very long time, but there is still sunrise and sunset.

Then you have areas where the sunrise and sunset is not quite dark, but it's twilight. And this is, for example, even in Scotland. In places in Scotland, I went to northern Scotland (is it Aberdeen or something?), and I remember clearly that you walk outside at 11 p.m., 11 p.m., and it's like what we think of as 6 p.m. over here. Twilight. It's not dark. You think it's Maghrib or a little bit after Maghrib, right? Well after Maghrib. But it's not going to go full dark over there. So that's far north. There is sunrise and sunset, but there's no darkness, and that's because you're in that twilight area, which is the civil or the nautical twilight. You are not in the astronomical; you don't get beyond that.

And then you have the furthest north, which is like Tromso, in which the sun does not even set or rise for months on end. For months, you'll see the sun just go in circles. You wake up at 3 a.m. to pray tahajjud, and the sun is outside, right? And six months later, you wake up at 3 p.m., and it is pitch black dark. And that's another scenario.

So what is to be done in all of these places? I'm just going to summarize the various opinions out there, and then I will conclude by telling you to not listen to me; listen to your local ulama. This is for information purposes. Know that all of these different fatwas are there. Whichever one you choose, alhamdulillah, ulama bigger than me have said them. This is a very difficult scenario, a very difficult scenario: which one is correct, which one is right, which one is wrong. Inshallah, they're all rewarded by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Follow your community and follow your local ulama. But for information purposes, what are some of the opinions out there?

So the majority opinion, in lands where there is actual sunrise and sunset, is that there is simply no other alternative: you must fast according to the sunrise and sunset. And this is the position of the majority of councils and ulama. And they say even if it goes to 20, 21, 22 hours, then that is the fast. However, if the fast is overwhelming to people (if they have difficult, laborious jobs, if a sister is pregnant, if, if, if), then obviously the burden for them, the burden to not fast, is much lower than it is for us, right? So if your land has a 20-hour-long fast and you're expected to work in the fields, that's your job, or your difficult situation, you're a pregnant lady, for example... If you are maybe in America and it's a 13-hour fast, you could do it. But that's like a 20-hour fast; you cannot do that. So we say the bar has been lowered. And if you're not able to do the 20-hour fast, then you make up in the month that is easier for you. After two, three months, four months, you make up the days that you could not fast.

But technically, if you're able to fast, you fast. And the default for most average men and women is that it is possible to fast 18, 19 hours. And this is actually done even as a fad, and as a technique for losing weight, called intermittent fasting, where people will maybe eat one meal a day, and it is fine. They will live like this. It is something that is not harmful to the body once the body becomes accustomed to it, for many people but not for all. So that is the majority position.

However, even in this there are dissenting voices. And the Majma' al-Fiqh al-Islami, which is one of the bodies that I look up to the most, actually also gives the exact same fatwa: that as long as there is actual sunrise and sunset, well, then we're going to have to go with sunrise and sunset, and even if it's long, that will be the fast. However, what is to be done if it is further north than that, where you don't actually have sunrise and sunset? This is where we have a number of opinions.

One of the scholars of the last generation, Shaykh Mustafa al-Zarqa, said that any time the fast is unreasonably long (and he didn't define unreasonably long, but he said even when there's sunrise and sunset, if it's 20 hours or something), in that case, he said, the people can follow Mecca. They can follow Mecca, or they can follow the closest Muslim land where the fasts are reasonable.

And the Majma' al-Fiqh al-Islami said that if there is no sunrise and sunset, then they should follow the closest land where there are Muslims residing, where there is sunrise and sunset, and that will become their timing. So if you are in North Norway and there's no sunrise and sunset, you will look to South Norway, Oslo for example. Oslo generally has sunrise and sunset. So you will look to Oslo and the timings of Oslo, or (I'm just giving an example) the timings of the city where there are Muslims and there is sunrise and sunset will become your timings north of that. And this is the fatwa of the Majma' al-Fiqh al-Islami, and it is the one that I personally am sympathetic to. But again, don't listen to me; listen to your local ulama.

And by the way, this fatwa is also the fatwa of the Dar al-Ifta of Saudi Arabia, and also my teacher Shaykh Ibn Uthaymeen, and also Shaykh Ibn Baz and others. They also give the same fatwa: that the people living in those lands where there is no sunrise and sunset should look to the closest lands south of them, the closest city south of them where there are Muslims residing and where fasting is taking place and there is sunrise and sunset, and take the timings from them.

Another scholar, Dr. Muhammad Hamidullah, a great 'alim of hadith and a person who authored many, many books and discovered many treatises, Dr. Muhammad Hamidullah had an interesting fatwa: that in those lands far north or whatnot, we should simply take a minimum and a maximum and do a cutoff beyond that. And for reasons beyond the scope of my lecture today, he said eight to sixteen. So eight hours is the minimum fast. Because you see, guys, we're talking about the long days, but do realize, in 15, 20 years, when Ramadan comes in December, literally no exaggeration, in some of these lands the fast is going to be two hours. So you have a full suhoor, and by the time it comes for iftar, it's like, "Yes, all right, I'm full, I don't need to eat," because you're going to have a full suhoor and then you're not going to eat for two hours.

So Shaykh Hamidullah said that just like the people have to suffer, then in the winter time we have to do something for them. So what did he suggest? He suggested you extend the smallest days to at least 8 hours, and you cut off the longest days to 16 hours. So if the fast is 22 hours, you say 16 for them: you start at suhoor whenever there is Fajr, and then 16 hours later you call it a day, until you get to the eight hours. That was his fatwa, and again, he has his reasons for that.

Another great scholar of the last generation, a great 'alim and a person who really did a lot for the Muslims of the ummah, Shaykh Faisal Mawlawi of Lebanon (he was a very learned author), said that in those lands in which the sun sets at least 12 degrees below the horizon, i.e. we're talking about the nautical twilight and the nautical dawn, they should simply follow the nautical and not the astronomical. And so he basically said: use the smallest degree possible and stick with that. And that's an interesting position.

Yet another opinion states that they should follow the timings of the sunrise and sunset of their own locality on the last day that there was an actual sunrise and sunset. So even in Tromso, even in that little village up there, there is a sunrise and sunset for a period of the year, and then for the bulk of the year it goes away. The last day there was an actual sunrise and sunset, they should take that and keep it as their fast until the next sunrise and sunset, and then that will be the next portion over there.

And then the final fatwa I will mention (and of course there are actually more than these) is the fatwa of the Dar al-Ifta of Egypt, which is connected with Azhar University as well. And the Dar al-Ifta of Egypt is perhaps the fatwa that is most commonly done by many of the Muslim communities up north. When I visited Tromso, they told me that this is the fatwa they were using back then. This is like seven years ago; I don't know if this is the situation now.

And the Dar al-Ifta of Egypt said that in those northern lands, the people should follow Mecca. And so the timing (and when I say the timings, I mean how long is the fast of Mecca: if it's 14 hours, 15 hours, 13 hours, however long it is; generally the fasts are around 14 hours, generally, in Arabia), so they should look at Mecca and the timing of Ramadan, how many hours is the fast. They then start from Fajr, whenever they're going to pray Fajr, and from that they simply add the timings of Mecca, 14 and a half hours if it is 14 and a half hours, and then they break over there. So they use that as an arbitrary reference, because they said Mecca is the holy city, and they have their reasons for doing so.

To conclude all of this, dear brothers and sisters: my position, I already explained to you which one I'm sympathetic to. But at the end of the day, **I do not advise you to follow me; I advise you to follow your local scholars of your lands, who live amongst you**, and who understand really the ramifications and the pros and cons of each of these positions, and who understand other things that I might not be able to see from my perspective. And at the end of the day, the unity of the Muslims is more important. Alhamdulillah, all of these positions are there; whichever position you follow, there is khayr and good in it. The most important thing: you fear Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala as much as you can.

And dear brothers and sisters, wherever you are in the world, if the fasting is really not possible for you medically, you will fall sick, a reputable doctor tells you that, if you have diabetes or something of this nature and you cannot fast for 17 hours, 20 hours, even if it's 12 hours and you're a diabetic and you cannot fast, remember, you then constitute a sick patient, and a sick patient by the explicit text of the Qur'an. Allah says in the Qur'an: if you are sick, then don't fast. Don't worry about fasting. If you become cured, make it up. If not, then you give a kaffarah. Do not make the religion more difficult. Fasting is an obligation for those who are capable of doing it. Therefore, if you're capable of doing it given your circumstances, alhamdulillah. If not, alhamdulillah, and there are alternatives that need to be done with that.
